newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican banker may have been a robbery victim.
newsitem.headline: Mexican banker may have been a robbery victim.

text.p: The brother of Mexico's finance minister may have been shot to death with his own gun as part of a botched robbery attempt, police said on Tuesday, downplaying speculation the murder was politically motivated.

Alejandro Ortiz Martinez, a 55-year-old bank official and brother of Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz, died on Saturday after being shot in the head twice in his Mercedes Benz in Mexico City's upscale Lomas de Chapultepec neighborhood.

After reconstructing the murder's events this week, police said they believed Ortiz tried to use his own 9 mm pistol to fend off the would-be robbers, who apparently seized the weapon and may have used it to kill him.

Although family members said Ortiz always carried a gun for protection, and had used it just weeks earlier to defend himself from a similar heist, no gun was found at the scene of the crime, suggesting the crooks took the weapon, police said.
"This reaffirms our hypothesis that it was an attempted robbery," Luis Roberto Gutierrez Flores, director of Mexico City's judicial police department, told Reuters.
"The criminals approach, he reaches for his gun (in the glove compartment) and the event turns violent."

Police said the two robbers, whose descriptions fit members of a well-known car-theft ring, were prowling for victims when they spotted Ortiz, who was waiting in his car outside his home for his wife as the men approached.
"It had nothing to do with who he was. It could have been any Pedro or Juan," Gutierrez said.

Many ordinary Mexicans, soured by high-profile political killings in the past few years, suspect the murder was more than a simple robbery, prompted by his brother's cabinet post or his own position at a leading Mexican bank.
The culprits fled without stealing the car and apparently had time to smoke a few cigarettes before the crime, suggesting they may have staked out Ortiz.

A Tuesday editorial in the influential Reforma newspaper said authorities were too hasty in discarding a political or revenge motive, considering the victim's relationship to the powerful finance minister.
But Gutierrez rejected a political motive and said true assassins would not have waited 20 minutes before approaching the victim.
